PdfPecker turns HTML and Markdown into PDF, and PDF pages into PNG, JPEG or WebP images, in .NET. It has its own HTML parser, CSS engine, layout engine, PDF writer and PDF renderer, so it never starts a browser, ships no native binaries and depends on nothing but the .NET base class library. These pages describe PdfPecker 1.7. using PdfPecker; byte[] pdf = HtmlToPdf.Convert("

Hello

World

"); File.WriteAllBytes("hello.pdf", pdf);
dotnet add package PdfPecker The package targets net8.0, net9.0 and net10.0, so it works on .NET 8 and later.

// String to bytes byte[] pdf = HtmlToPdf.Convert(html); // String to a stream using (var file = File.Create("out.pdf")) HtmlToPdf.Convert(html, file); // ASP.NET Core app.MapGet("/invoice", () => Results.File(HtmlToPdf.Convert(html), "application/pdf", "invoice.pdf")); // File to file; relative and paths resolve against the HTML file's folder HtmlToPdf.ConvertFile("invoice.html", "invoice.pdf"); // Off the calling thread byte[] pdf = await HtmlToPdf.ConvertAsync(html); All methods are static and thread-safe, so you can convert many documents in parallel. Page size, margins, headers, footers and the rest are set with PdfOptions.

Required: the .NET 8, .NET 9 or .NET 10 runtime (or later). Nothing else: the library is pure managed code with no native binaries, browser or third-party packages, so it runs wherever .NET runs (Windows, Linux, macOS; x64 and ARM64). The rendered pages are the same on every version; only the compressed bytes can differ, because each .NET version ships its own zlib build. Recommended: Register the fonts your templates use with options.Fonts (see Fonts); other fonts fall back to Helvetica, Times or Courier metrics. Memory and CPU are small. Measured on a 4-core 2.1 GHz Xeon cloud VM (Linux, .NET 10, Release), each document in a fresh process: Document Pages Time, warm Time, first in process Peak process memory Smallest heap that works Payslip, invoice, voucher 1 to 3 1 to 3 ms 0.2 s 50 MB under 16 MB Same with PDF/A or embedded fonts 1 to 3 3 to 5 ms 0.2 s 56 MB under 16 MB Report with tables 30 30 to 40 ms 0.3 s 75 MB under 16 MB Report with tables 1,000 1.7 s 3 s 480 MB 245 MB The process itself starts at about 32 MB; a conversion uses about one core, so throughput grows with cores. PDF/A and font embedding add a few milliseconds and about 5 MB for the embedded font data. Memory grows roughly with page count, so plan about 0.5 MB per page for very long documents. From a clone of the PdfPecker repository, dotnet run --project bench/PdfPecker.Benchmarks -c Release -- --requirements [your.html ...] measures this on your own machine and documents.

Options: page size, margins, headers and footers, document properties and file access. HTML and CSS support and Paged media: what your templates can use. Fonts: register your own fonts and use any Unicode text. Limitations: what PdfPecker does not do (yet).

PdfOptions controls the page, the document properties and how resources are loaded. Every conversion method takes one; leave it out for A4 pages with the defaults below. var options = new PdfOptions { PageSize = PageSize.Letter.Landscape, // A3, A4 (default), A5, Letter, Legal or new PageSize(w, h) in points Margins = PageMargins.FromMillimeters(20, 15, 20, 15), Scale = 1, // like Chrome's print scale (see its docs to match IronPDF's output) TruncateBandsToWholePoints = false, // round header/footer height attributes down to whole points, as Chrome does BaseDirectory = "/var/app/templates", // where relative image/stylesheet paths are resolved ResourceResolver = url => myCache.Get(url), // serve http(s) or embedded resources yourself; null = default handling UserStyleSheet = "body { font-size: 10pt }", // extra CSS applied after the document's own FooterText = "Page {page} of {pages}", // also HeaderText Title = "Invoice 42", Author = "Accounts", // document properties (Title defaults to <title>) Keywords = "invoice", Creator = "MyApp", // also Subject, and Producer (default "PdfPecker") CustomProperties = { ["RunId"] = "42" }, // your own properties, in the PDF's document information Bookmarks = true, // PDF bookmarks from h1-h6 (default) FormFields = true, // inputs, selects and textareas become fillable fields (default) Compress = true, // Flate-compress page content (default) AllowFileAccess = false, // true: also read files outside BaseDirectory (trusted HTML only) MaxPages = 1000, // refuse longer documents with PdfLimitException (default 100,000) }; byte[] pdf = HtmlToPdf.Convert(html, options);

Local images and stylesheets are read only from inside BaseDirectory (the input file's folder for ConvertFile): absolute paths, file: URLs, .. and symbolic links that lead outside it are ignored unless AllowFileAccess = true, and converting a string without a BaseDirectory reads no files at all. For HTML from untrusted users, keep it that way, set a low MaxPages, and pass a cancellation token with a timeout (HtmlToPdf.Convert(html, options, token)): cancelling stops the conversion where it is.

A CSS @page { size: A4 landscape; margin: 15mm } rule overrides the page size and margins unless IgnoreCssPageRules is set. PdfPecker never makes network requests on its own: http(s) images and stylesheets are only loaded through ResourceResolver.

Custom properties are written to the document information dictionary, where Acrobat shows them under Document Properties > Custom and pdfinfo -custom lists them. For PDF/A they are also written to the XMP metadata (Acrobat's pdfx namespace, with the extension schema PDF/A requires), alongside Keywords, Creator and Producer.

The other options have pages of their own: Fonts, EmbedStandardFonts, MissingFont and MissingCharacter, Language and Hyphenation, Watermark, Security and Conformance, Accessibility, EInvoice, Attachments, Signature and FormFields.
PdfPecker lays out HTML and CSS the way Chrome prints it. Anything not listed here should be assumed missing; the known gaps are listed under Limitations.

The common document elements: headings, paragraphs, div/section-style blocks, span, a (external links and #id links inside the document), b/strong, i/em, u, s, sub, sup, small, big, mark, code, pre, blockquote, hr, br, ul/ol/li (nested, with start and value), dl, table (with thead, tbody, tfoot, caption, colspan, rowspan, col width), img, inline <svg>, and legacy attributes such as align, valign, bgcolor, width, height, border, cellpadding, cellspacing and <font>. The dir attribute (ltr, rtl and auto), <bdi> and <bdo> set the text direction. The parser is forgiving about unclosed and misnested tags, the way browsers are. Markdown is converted to this HTML first; see Markdown.

Lines, images and table rows are never cut in half at a page boundary; table header rows repeat on every page a table spans; backgrounds and borders continue across pages. Flex lines and grid rows move to the next page as a whole when they don't fit. A paragraph that splits leaves at least orphans lines (default 2) at the bottom of a page and carries at least widows lines (default 2) to the next. Headings keep with the content that follows them (break-after: avoid in the default styles), and break-before/break-after: avoid does the same for any block. break-inside: avoid keeps a block or a whole table on one page when it fits.

<a href> becomes a clickable link, whether inline or a block (a card wrapped in a link), and stays clickable on both pages when a page break splits it. External URLs open in the viewer's browser and #id links jump to the element. Headings h1-h6 become the PDF's bookmarks, nested by level; set PdfOptions.Bookmarks = false to leave them out.

Inline and as url() backgrounds, including data:image/svg+xml URIs) with path (all commands, arcs included), rect (incl. rounded), circle, ellipse, line, polyline, polygon, text and tspan (x, y, dx, dy, text-anchor, dominant-baseline, direction, registered fonts and right-to-left text), g, use, nested svg, viewBox, preserveAspectRatio and transform, drawn as vector paths. linearGradient and radialGradient (both units, gradientTransform, spreadMethod, href inheritance) become PDF shadings, and pattern fills and strokes (both units, viewBox, patternTransform, href inheritance) become PDF tiling patterns. clipPath clips the elements that reference it, and mask (luminance or alpha, both units) becomes a PDF soft mask. marker draws arrowheads and dots at the vertices of paths, lines, polylines and polygons (orient incl. auto and auto-start-reverse, markerUnits, viewBox, refX/refY, clipped to the marker unless overflow="visible"). filter is applied in pixels, at 144 dpi, and drawn as an image: feGaussianBlur, feOffset, feDropShadow, feFlood, feMerge, feComposite (all operators), feBlend (separable modes), feColorMatrix, feComponentTransfer and feMorphology, in linearRGB or sRGB. As in browsers, an SVG file is styled only by its own

JPEG (embedded as-is, RGB, grayscale and CMYK), PNG (all colour types and bit depths, transparency, interlacing), GIF (transparency, interlacing) and WebP (lossy, lossless and with alpha), from files, data: URIs or your ResourceResolver. Animated GIF and WebP files show their first frame. SVG files are drawn as vectors (see SVG above). Opaque PNGs are passed through without re-encoding. Images wider than the page are scaled down to fit.

@page rules set the page size, margins and background, and their margin boxes (@top-left, @top-center, @bottom-right and the other thirteen) print headers and footers with counter(page) and counter(pages), chosen per page with :first, :left and :right. On top of that: Named pages: page: wide puts an element on pages styled by @page wide { ... }, with their own size, orientation, margins, background and margin boxes. Content on another named page starts a new page, so a landscape table or a full-bleed cover can sit between portrait pages. Running headers: string-set copies text from the document (content(), attr(), strings and counters) into a named string, and string(name) shows it in a margin box: the chapter title in the page header, say. As in the spec, string(name, first | start | last | first-except) picks which value a page shows. Tables of contents: target-counter(attr(href), page) shows the page number of the element a link points to, and leader(dotted) (or solid, space, or a string) fills the space before it. target-text() shows the linked element's text. The document is laid out again with the numbers it finds, so they are always right. @page { size: A4; margin: 20mm; @top-center { content: string(chapter) } @bottom-right { content: "Page " counter(page) " of " counter(pages) } } @page cover { margin: 0; background: #1d3557; @top-center { content: none } @bottom-right { content: none } } @page wide { size: A4 landscape } .cover { page: cover } .wide-table { page: wide } h2 { string-set: chapter content(); break-before: page } nav a::after { content: leader(dotted) target-counter(attr(href), page) } Chrome supports named pages and margin boxes, but not running strings, target-counter() or leader().

h: Running header and footer from HTML
x: An element with the data-sticky-pdf-header or data-sticky-pdf-footer attribute is taken out of the flow and drawn at the top or bottom of every page, and the page content flows in the space between. Inside it, {page} and {total-pages} (or {pages}) are replaced with the page number and page count. An optional height attribute (height="17mm") reserves at least that much space. <header data-sticky-pdf-header height="17mm">ACME Ltd · Payslip</header> <main>...</main> <footer data-sticky-pdf-footer height="12mm">Page {page} of {total-pages}</footer>

Markdown goes to PDF through the same engine as HTML: it is turned into HTML with a GitHub-like stylesheet first, so everything on HTML and CSS support applies to it. You can also stop at the HTML. // Markdown to PDF, styled like a GitHub README byte[] pdf = MarkdownToPdf.Convert(File.ReadAllText("README.md")); // File to file; relative image paths resolve against the Markdown file's folder MarkdownToPdf.ConvertFile("README.md", "README.pdf", new PdfOptions { FooterText = "Page {page} of {pages}" }); // Markdown to HTML: a body fragment, or a complete page with the stylesheet string fragment = MarkdownToHtml.Convert("# Hello *World*"); //

string page = MarkdownToHtml.ConvertDocument(markdown); MarkdownToHtml.ConvertFile("README.md", "README.html"); MarkdownOptions switches the GitHub extensions off for strict CommonMark (GitHubExtensions = false), drops heading ids (HeadingIds = false), shows raw HTML as text (AllowRawHtml = false), replaces the stylesheet (StyleSheet, see MarkdownToHtml.DefaultStyleSheet) or sets the title (default: the first heading). MarkdownToPdf takes PdfOptions and MarkdownOptions side by side.

CommonMark 0.31 (651 of the 652 spec examples pass; the one miss is an exotic HTML5 entity name) plus the GitHub Flavored Markdown extensions: tables with column alignment, ~~strikethrough~~, task list items (- [x]) and bare www./https:///e-mail autolinks. Headings get GitHub-style ids, so [see below](#heading-text) links work in the PDF too. The parser runs in linear time on hostile input (deep nesting, unclosed brackets, long delimiter runs). See Limitations for what is not supported.

Register TrueType or OpenType fonts and use them by name in CSS. Only the glyphs a document uses are embedded, and text can use any Unicode character the fonts have (Greek, Cyrillic, Central European, CJK, ...): var options = new PdfOptions(); options.Fonts.AddFile("fonts/OpenSans-Regular.ttf") .AddFile("fonts/OpenSans-Bold.ttf"); // family, weight and style are read from the files options.Fonts.Add(bytes, familyName: "sans-serif"); // or override a generic family options.Fonts.AddDirectory(@"C:\Windows\Fonts"); // read once, loaded only when used byte[] pdf = HtmlToPdf.Convert("

Łódź, Ελλάδα, Москва

", options);

Documents can bring their own fonts with @font-face (files, data: URIs or ResourceResolver URLs; local() refers to registered fonts): @font-face { font-family: Brand; src: url(fonts/brand.woff2) format("woff2"); font-weight: 400; } @font-face { font-family: Brand; src: url(fonts/brand-bold.ttf); font-weight: 700; unicode-range: U+0000-024F; } A FontCollection can be shared between options and parallel conversions. Formats: .ttf, .otf, .ttc collections, WOFF and WOFF2 (including WOFF2 collections; decoded with .NET's built-in Brotli). Fonts are matched like browsers do: by family, then style, then the nearest weight; a missing bold or italic face is synthesized. A character that the chosen font lacks is drawn with the next font in the font-family list that has it, then the standard font, then any other registered font.

Variable fonts (one file with a weight, width, slant or other axis, with TrueType or CFF2 outlines) work with the usual CSS properties. PdfPecker builds a static instance of the font, with its kerning, for each combination a document uses and embeds a subset of it, so bold text uses the font's real bold rather than a synthesized one: @font-face { font-family: Inter; src: url(fonts/InterVariable.ttf); } /* covers all of the font's weights */ h1 { font-family: Inter; font-weight: 750; } .narrow { font-stretch: 75%; } /* the wdth axis */ em { font-style: italic; } /* the ital axis, or slnt */ .custom { font-variation-settings: "wght" 650, "GRAD" 50; } /* any axis, overrides the rest */ A variable @font-face without font-weight covers the font's whole weight range, and so does a variable font added through options.Fonts. A face declared with a single weight (font-weight: 400) stays at that weight, and bold is synthesized as for any other font. The optical size axis (opsz) follows the font size unless font-optical-sizing: none is set. CFF2 fonts are embedded as ordinary CFF fonts, since few PDF readers can draw CFF2.

Text without a registered font uses the standard PDF fonts (Helvetica, Times, Courier), which viewers supply themselves, so files stay small but are limited to Western European characters. Set EmbedStandardFonts = true to embed the bundled Liberation fonts in their place instead: they have the same widths, so the layout does not change, the text looks the same in every viewer, and any character they cover (Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, ...) works. PDF/A always does this. It adds a subset of each font used to the file (typically 10-25 KB per font).

A family that no font provides falls back silently, like in a browser. To notice, set MissingFont: it is called once per conversion for each family that had to be substituted, and throwing from it fails the conversion. To use the fonts installed on the machine for families you have not registered, set UseSystemFonts = true (off by default, so the output does not depend on the machine): options.MissingFont = family => logger.LogWarning("Font {Family} is not available", family); options.UseSystemFonts = true; // looks in C:\Windows\Fonts, /Library/Fonts, /usr/share/fonts, ... Likewise, a character that no font has is drawn as an empty box (blank space in PDF/A). MissingCharacter is called once for each such character before anything is written, so a test can make sure a template's fonts cover its data: options.MissingCharacter = ch => throw new InvalidOperationException($"No font has U+{char.ConvertToUtf32(ch, 0):X4}");

Registered and @font-face TrueType/OpenType fonts are embedded as subsets (Type0/CIDFontType2 for TrueType outlines, CIDFontType0 with an OpenType program for CFF outlines) with a ToUnicode map, so text can be searched and copied. Without them, the PDF standard fonts are used: font-family maps to Helvetica (sans-serif, Arial, Verdana, ...), Times (serif, Georgia, ...) or Courier (monospace, Consolas, ...), each in regular, bold, italic and bold italic. With EmbedStandardFonts or PDF/A, these are replaced by embedded subsets of the bundled, metric-compatible Liberation Sans, Serif and Mono.

Arabic and Hebrew are laid out right to left and shaped like browsers do, with PdfPecker's own implementation of the Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm (UAX #9, passing all of Unicode's conformance tests) and of OpenType shaping (GSUB and GPOS, following HarfBuzz). Arabic letters join, lam-alef and other ligatures form, and harakat and Hebrew points are placed on their letters by the font's mark positioning. Mixed text (an English product name or a number inside an Arabic sentence) is put in the right order, and brackets are mirrored. Register a font that has the script, then set the direction with the dir attribute or CSS direction: var options = new PdfOptions(); options.Fonts.AddFile("fonts/NotoNaskhArabic-Regular.ttf"); byte[] pdf = HtmlToPdf.Convert("""

فاتورة رقم ٢٠٢٦/١٥

المبلغ الإجمالي: 1,250.00 DKK

""", options); In a right-to-left block, text aligns right (text-align: start), and table columns, flex rows, grid columns and list markers run from the right. dir="auto", and work as in browsers, and so do unicode-bidi, text-align: start/end and the logical margin and padding properties (margin-inline-start, padding-inline-end, ...). text-overflow: ellipsis and line-clamp cut right-to-left lines at their left end. SVG is reordered and shaped too, with direction deciding which way a text chunk runs from its x. Copied or extracted text gives back the original characters in logical order. A font without OpenType Arabic features is shaped with the Unicode presentation forms instead.

hyphens: auto hyphenates words with the TeX hyphenation patterns (Liang's algorithm) of the text's language: the nearest lang attribute, else PdfOptions.Language. As in Chrome, a word is hyphenated only where it does not fit on its line, and a hyphen (or the hyphenate-character) is shown at the break. Words shorter than five letters, words with digits or other non-letters inside, URLs and e-mail addresses, and capitalized English words are not hyphenated, and a word with ­ breaks only there. Patterns for English (US patterns for every en tag), Danish, German, Dutch and Norwegian (nb, nn, no) are built in and loaded on first use; others can be supplied as TeX pattern files, such as those of the hyph-utf8 project: var options = new PdfOptions { // Your own patterns for a language (they take precedence over the built-in ones). Hyphenation = new Dictionary { ["sv"] = new HyphenationPatterns(File.ReadAllText("hyph-sv.tex"), leftMin: 2, rightMin: 2), }, }; byte[] pdf = HtmlToPdf.Convert("""

Arbejdsmarkedsbidraget betales af lønmodtageren.

""", options);

var options = new PdfOptions { // A diagonal stamp on every page. Also: Image (PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP bytes), FontSize, LetterSpacing, Angle, Opacity, Bold, Behind. Watermark = new PdfWatermark { Text = "WATERMARK", Color = "#c00000", Opacity = 0.25f }, // AES-256 encryption (PDF 2.0 / Acrobat X and later). Without an OwnerPassword a random one is used, // so the permissions cannot be lifted. Security = new PdfSecurity { UserPassword = "1234", // needed to open the file; null = opens freely OwnerPassword = "owner-secret", // full access Permissions = PdfPermissions.Print | PdfPermissions.Copy, }, };

For archiving, set Conformance = PdfConformance.PdfA2b (or another level below): the PDF gets XMP metadata, an sRGB output intent and a file ID, and CMYK JPEGs are converted to RGB. All fonts are embedded: text without a registered font uses the bundled Liberation fonts (see Fonts). PDF/A does not allow encryption, so combining Conformance with Security throws an ArgumentException. var options = new PdfOptions { Conformance = PdfConformance.PdfA4 }; Level Standard File Use it for PdfA2b, PdfA3b ISO 19005-2/-3, level B PDF 1.7 the usual archive format; part 3 also allows attachments (e-invoices) PdfA2u, PdfA3u ISO 19005-2/-3, level U PDF 1.7 as level B, plus a Unicode mapping for every character, so text can be searched and copied PdfA4 ISO 19005-4:2020 PDF 2.0 the current part; identified in the XMP only (pdfaid:rev 2020, no conformance letter), no document information dictionary PdfA4f ISO 19005-4:2020, with files PDF 2.0 PDF/A-4 with attachments: only with EInvoice (it throws without one) Every font is embedded with a ToUnicode map, and a character no font has is left out as blank space rather than drawn as .notdef (in SVG text too), so levels U cost nothing over B. A PDF 2.0 file keeps the title, author, keywords and custom properties in its XMP metadata, since PDF 2.0 deprecates the information dictionary. Every level, on its own and with PDF/UA, passes veraPDF 1.28 (flavours 2b, 2u, 3b, 3u, 4 and 4f) on documents with text, tables, lists, images, links, form fields, SVG and Markdown. AES-256 keys come from a password hash that is slow on purpose, which adds about 3 ms to a conversion.

To add, change or remove the password of a PDF you already have (from any producer, not only PdfPecker), use PdfProtector: // Encrypt any PDF with AES-256 byte[] locked = PdfProtector.Encrypt(pdf, new PdfSecurity { UserPassword = "1234", Permissions = PdfPermissions.Print }); // Change the passwords or permissions of an encrypted PDF (give its current user or owner password) byte[] relocked = PdfProtector.Encrypt(locked, new PdfSecurity { UserPassword = "5678" }, password: "1234"); // Remove the encryption, and with it the permission restrictions byte[] open = PdfProtector.Decrypt(locked, "1234"); // Stream overloads, and a check PdfProtector.Encrypt(inputStream, outputStream, security); bool encrypted = PdfProtector.IsEncrypted(pdf); Encrypted inputs can use RC4 (40 to 128 bit), AES-128 or AES-256; the output of Encrypt is always AES-256. Like other PDF tools, PdfProtector accepts the user password as well as the owner password (or none, for a file that only restricts permissions), so anyone who can open a document can also lift its permissions. A wrong password throws PdfPasswordException. The document is rewritten as a whole and keeps its pages, bookmarks, links, form fields and values, tags, metadata, page labels and attachments; earlier revisions from incremental updates are dropped. Signed PDFs are refused with an ArgumentException (rewriting them would break the signatures; sign after encrypting instead), as is encrypting a PDF/A file, or a PDF/UA file without PdfPermissions.ExtractForAccessibility. Decrypt returns a PDF that is not encrypted unchanged. Watermark applies while converting HTML; to stamp a PDF you already have, see Stamping PDFs.

var options = new PdfOptions { Accessibility = PdfAccessibility.PdfUA1, // or PdfUA2, or Tagged: the same structure without the PDF/UA claim Language = "da", // default: <html lang="...">; for PDF/UA without either, "en" Conformance = PdfConformance.PdfA2b, // optional: PDF/UA-1 combines with PDF/A-2 and 3, PDF/UA-2 with PDF/A-4 };

Tagged gives the PDF a structure tree built from the HTML, so screen readers, reflow and text extraction follow the document rather than the page layout: headings (H1 to H6), paragraphs, lists with their labels, tables with header scopes and spans, figures with their alt text, links (tied to their clickable areas), block quotes, code and sections, all in document order, with lang attributes as the language of the element. Text outside a paragraph (straight in a div, say) gets one. Backgrounds, borders, running headers and footers, HeaderText/FooterText, watermarks, repeated table headers, fixed boxes and decorative images are artifacts that assistive technology skips.

PdfUA1 adds what ISO 14289-1 asks beyond the tags: every font embedded (the bundled Liberation fonts stand in for the standard ones), the title shown in the viewer's title bar and the PDF/UA identification in the XMP metadata. The output passes veraPDF's PDF/UA-1 checks, on its own and together with PDF/A-2b or PDF/A-3b (e-invoices included). It needs a title: Title, the <title> element or else the first heading; without one, conversion throws ArgumentException, as it does when Security leaves out PdfPermissions.ExtractForAccessibility.

PdfUA2 (ISO 14289-2:2024) is the PDF 2.0 successor: the file is written as PDF 2.0, its tags are in the PDF 2.0 structure namespace (block quotes, quotes and code, which PDF 2.0 dropped, keep their PDF 1.7 type and are role mapped to Div and Span), links and bookmarks go to structure destinations (the element they point at, not only its page), lists state their numbering and form fields describe themselves, and the XMP says pdfuaid:part 2 with pdfuaid:rev 2024. It has the same title and language requirements as PdfUA1 and passes veraPDF's PDF/UA-2 checks, on its own and with PdfA4. PDF/UA-1 and PDF/A-2 and 3 are based on PDF 1.7, PDF/UA-2 and PDF/A-4 on PDF 2.0, so PdfUA2 with PdfA2b (or any PDF/A-2 or 3 level) and PdfUA1 with PdfA4 throw ArgumentException.

What the tags can't fix is up to the HTML: give images an alt (an image without alt, aria-label or title, or an <svg> without a <title>, counts as decorative), use real headings, lists and th cells, and mark purely visual content aria-hidden="true". Heading levels that skip one (h1 then h3) are tagged one level below the previous heading, as PDF/UA does not allow gaps.

Form controls become fillable PDF form fields (AcroForm), drawn as Chrome prints them and filled with their current values. Adobe Reader, Preview, Chrome, Firefox and other viewers let the reader fill them in and save the result. var html = """

Name

S M

"""; byte[] pdf = HtmlToPdf.Convert(html); // Or print the controls as they are, without form fields: byte[] flat = HtmlToPdf.Convert(html, new PdfOptions { FormFields = false }); HTML PDF field of type text, email, tel, url, search, number, date and the like Text field (maxlength sets the maximum length) Password text field; the value is drawn as dots and not stored

Fields are named after the name attribute (a period becomes _, since PDF uses it to nest fields; a repeated name gets _2, _3, ...; a control without a name gets text1, checkbox1, ...). readonly and required set the field's flags, title, aria-label or its <label> becomes its tooltip, and a placeholder is drawn in grey while the field is empty. Disabled controls (or controls in a disabled <fieldset>) are drawn but not fillable, and hidden inputs are left out. Each field has its own appearance, so the PDF looks right before anyone touches it and in viewers that never redraw fields; while a field is edited, the viewer draws its text in Helvetica, Courier or Times at the control's size and colour. Forms work with Security (the values are encrypted with the rest), Conformance (veraPDF passes the fields as PDF/A-2b and 3b), Accessibility (each widget sits in a Form element described by its label, title or name, and veraPDF passes PDF/UA-1), Signature (the signature field joins the form) and PdfMerger (repeated names are renamed).

Sign the PDF with a certificate (a .pfx file or one from the certificate store). Adobe Reader then shows who signed it and whether the file was changed afterwards. var cert = X509CertificateLoader.LoadPkcs12FromFile("signer.pfx", "pfx-password"); var options = new PdfOptions { Signature = new PdfSignatureOptions(cert) { Reason = "Approved", Location = "Copenhagen", // Optional: a visible box (points from the top-left corner; Page = -1 is the last page). Appearance = new PdfSignatureAppearance { Page = -1, X = 340, Y = 720, Width = 220, Height = 70 }, // Optional: a trusted RFC 3161 timestamp (PAdES B-T). The only option that uses the network. TimestampUrl = "http://timestamp.digicert.com", }, }; // Or sign any existing PDF; earlier signatures stay valid. byte[] signed = PdfSigner.Sign(File.ReadAllBytes("in.pdf"), new PdfSignatureOptions(cert)); // A contract template with empty signature fields: sign into one by name, at its place on the page. byte[] countersigned = PdfSigner.Sign(contract, new PdfSignatureOptions(cert) { FieldName = "Buyer" });

When FieldName names an empty signature field the PDF already has ("Parties.Buyer" for a nested one), the signature goes into it and the box fills the field's rectangle; signing a field of another type or one that is already signed throws PdfSignatureException. Any other name adds a new field.

Signatures are PAdES baseline (ETSI.CAdES.detached) by default, or classic adbe.pkcs7.detached with Format = PdfSignatureFormat.Pkcs7Detached; RSA and ECDSA keys with SHA-256/384/512. The signature is appended as an incremental update, and it works together with Security (encrypted files) and Conformance (PDF/A: the visible box is drawn as outlines, so it needs no unembedded font). The CMS structure is built with .NET's own System.Formats.Asn1 and System.Security.Cryptography; no extra package is needed. Signing adds a few milliseconds (the RSA or ECDSA operation and re-reading the file); conversions without a signature are unaffected.

Pass the invoice's CII XML (from your invoicing system) and PdfPecker attaches it to the PDF, making a Factur-X / ZUGFeRD e-invoice: the pages are the human-readable invoice and the XML is what accounting software reads. var options = new PdfOptions { EInvoice = new PdfEInvoice(File.ReadAllBytes("invoice.xml")), }; File.WriteAllBytes("invoice.pdf", HtmlToPdf.Convert(invoiceHtml, options)); The file is PDF/A-3b, so Conformance is raised to PdfA3b when it is left at None; PdfA3u and PdfA4f (PDF/A-4 with attachments) work too, while the other levels and Security throw. Factur-X and ZUGFeRD specify PDF/A-3, so keep the default unless the receiver asks for PDF/A-4f. The XML is embedded unchanged as factur-x.xml (xrechnung.xml for XRechnung), listed as an associated file, and the XMP metadata gets the Factur-X extension schema with the document type, version and profile. The profile (MINIMUM, BASIC WL, BASIC, EN 16931, EXTENDED or XRECHNUNG) is read from the XML's guideline ID; pass it as the second constructor argument to set it yourself. The relationship to the pages defaults to Data for MINIMUM and BASIC WL and Alternative otherwise; set Relationship to change it. PdfPecker checks that the XML is a well-formed Cross Industry Invoice (UBL is not allowed in Factur-X) but does not validate its content or build it from invoice data: make sure the visible pages show the same invoice. The output passes the Mustang validator (PDF/A-3b via veraPDF, and the XML's schematron). Other files can be attached next to the invoice with Attachments (see Attachments).

h: PDF attachments in UBL e-invoices (Peppol, OIOUBL)
x: Peppol BIS Billing 3.0, OIOUBL, EHF, XRechnung UBL and other UBL e-invoices are XML only: the XML is the invoice, and the PDF travels inside it as an attachment. UblInvoice.AttachPdf adds one to the invoice or credit note your invoicing system made: byte[] pdf = HtmlToPdf.Convert(invoiceHtml); byte[] xml = UblInvoice.AttachPdf(File.ReadAllBytes("invoice.xml"), pdf, "INV-1001.pdf"); The PDF goes in as an AdditionalDocumentReference with EmbeddedDocumentBinaryObject (mimeCode="application/pdf" and the file name), after any attachments already there and where the UBL schema expects it. The rest of the XML, including its indentation, encoding and declaration, is kept as it was. The reference ID defaults to the file name; pass id and description to set them. For OIOUBL 2.1 (UBL 2.0) the description is written as the DocumentType OIOUBL requires, PDF by default. The output passes the UBL schemas, the Peppol BIS 3.0 and EN 16931 schematrons, and the OIOUBL 2.1 schematron. PdfPecker does not build or validate the rest of the invoice.

Any file can travel inside the PDF, listed in the viewer's attachments panel: the source spreadsheet of a report, the data behind a chart, a signed contract. var options = new PdfOptions { Conformance = PdfConformance.PdfA3b }; // optional options.Attachments.Add(new PdfAttachment("figures.csv", csvBytes) { Description = "The figures behind the charts", // default: the file name Relationship = PdfAttachmentRelationship.Data, // Source, Data, Alternative, Supplement or Unspecified // MimeType = "text/csv", // default: guessed from the extension // CreationDate = ..., ModDate = ... // default: ModDate is the time of conversion }); options.Attachments.Add(PdfAttachment.FromFile("contract.pdf")); byte[] pdf = HtmlToPdf.Convert(html, options); // Read them back, or attach files to a PDF made elsewhere. foreach (PdfAttachment a in PdfAttachments.List(pdf)) Console.WriteLine($"{a.FileName}: {a.Data.Length} bytes"); byte[]? csv = PdfAttachments.Extract(pdf, "figures.csv"); byte[] more = PdfAttachments.Add(File.ReadAllBytes("scan.pdf"), new PdfAttachment("notes.txt", notes));

Each file is written with its MIME type, size, dates and MD5 checksum, in the document's embedded-files list sorted by name, and as an associated file (/AF) with its relationship to the pages, as PDF/A-3 requires. File names must be unique (ArgumentException otherwise; an attachment can't take the e-invoice's factur-x.xml). Attachments don't change Conformance: without one the file is a plain PDF, PDF/A-3b, PDF/A-3u and PDF/A-4f allow any attachment, and PDF/A-2b, PDF/A-2u and PDF/A-4, which allow only PDF/A files as attachments, throw ArgumentException rather than produce a file that fails validation. With Security the attachments are encrypted with the rest of the file, and for PDF/UA each one gets the description ISO 14289 asks for. The output passes veraPDF's PDF/A-3b, PDF/A-3u, PDF/A-4f, PDF/UA-1 and PDF/UA-2 checks. PdfAttachments.Add likewise refuses PDF/A-1, PDF/A-2 and PDF/A-4 files, and adds to PDF/A-3 and PDF/A-4f files.

PdfAttachments.Add appends the files as an incremental update, so the original bytes, and any digital signatures over them, stay as they were; an encrypted PDF (pass its password) stays encrypted, a PDF/A-3 file gets the new associated files, and PDF/A-1 and PDF/A-2 files are refused. List and Extract read the embedded-files list and associated files of any PDF, decrypting with the password you pass; files attached to page annotations (the paper-clip icons) are not read.

PdfMerger combines PDFs into one, any PDFs, not only those PdfPecker made: byte[] merged = PdfMerger.Merge(invoicePdf, termsPdf, attachmentPdf); // With passwords for encrypted inputs (by position), and properties for the result. byte[] merged2 = PdfMerger.Merge(new[] { a, b }, new PdfMergeOptions { Passwords = new string?[] { null, "secret" }, Title = "Payslips October", CustomProperties = { ["RunId"] = "42" }, }); PdfMerger.MergeFiles("all.pdf", new[] { "a.pdf", "b.pdf" }); // Streams in and out: inputs are read one at a time and the result is written as it is made. PdfMerger.Merge(new[] { invoiceStream, termsStream }, outputStream); await PdfMerger.MergeAsync(uploads.Select(f => f.OpenReadStream()), response.Body); Tagged inputs stay tagged: their structure trees are joined under one root, so the merged file is still accessible, and when every input is PDF/UA-1 the result says so too (veraPDF passes it). The merged file is PDF 1.7, so PDF/UA-2 inputs stay tagged but the result claims no PDF/UA level. An input in another language than the first keeps its language on its own part of the tree. Untagged inputs merge as before. With streams (and MergeFiles), only one input is held in memory at a time and the merged document goes to the output as each input is done, so memory follows the largest input rather than the whole batch: merging 100 files of 32 MB in total peaks at 14 MB of managed memory, against 105 MB with byte arrays. MergeAsync reads and writes asynchronously, as ASP.NET Core requires for request and response bodies. Input streams are read from their current position and are not disposed; the sequence is enumerated lazily, so an iterator can open each one only when its turn comes. MergeFiles writes to a temporary file and moves it into place, so the output can be one of the inputs and a failed merge leaves no partial file behind.

For PDFs that arrive one at a time from elsewhere, such as downloads read a few at a time, use StreamingPdfMerger. It writes each PDF's pages when it is added and then lets the PDF go, so memory stays at about one input, and between inputs you decide what comes next: skip a missing document, or check that anything was added before answering. The output can be an HTTP response body or a file; it does not need to be seekable. var merger = new StreamingPdfMerger(response.Body, new PdfMergeOptions { Title = "Payslips October" }); foreach (var path in paths) { var pdf = await storage.DownloadAsync(path, ct); if (pdf.Length == 0) continue; // skip a missing document await merger.AddAsync(pdf, ct); } if (merger.InputCount == 0) return Results.NotFound(); await merger.CompleteAsync(ct); // writes the page tree, bookmarks, form and cross-reference table // Or, from an IAsyncEnumerable<byte[]>: int pages = await PdfMerger.MergeAsync(DownloadInOrder(paths), response.Body, cancellationToken: ct); The result is the same as PdfMerger.Merge's, but the output is only a valid PDF once Complete has run. If adding a PDF throws (a damaged or encrypted input, MaxPages reached), what was written cannot be used and the merger refuses further calls. Passwords are matched to inputs in the order they are added. The pages keep their content, fonts, images, links, annotations, layers and fillable form fields, and each input's bookmarks follow each other. A form field named like one in an earlier input is renamed name_2, name_3 and so on, so the copies keep their own values. Document properties come from the first input unless PdfMergeOptions sets them. The result is never encrypted (pass it to PdfProtector.Encrypt to protect it) and has no signatures (merging would break them); PDF/A conformance is not carried over. Page labels are kept (pages of an input without them are numbered as in that input), and attachments too, with one named like an earlier input's listed as name (2).ext. Images, fonts and other resources that are byte-for-byte the same in several inputs, such as a logo on every payslip of a run, are written once. Inputs are handled as untrusted: damaged files are repaired where possible, decoding is limited per input, and MaxPages (default 100,000) caps the result. Inputs without any pages throw InvalidDataException. Merging was tested on PDFs from Chrome (as IronPDF makes them), Ghostscript, LibreOffice, MuPDF, qpdf, ReportLab, pypdf incremental updates, scanners (JPEG, CCITT G4, CMYK, OCR text layers) and damaged files (wrong or missing cross-reference tables, truncated files, junk before the header); every merged page rendered pixel-identical to its original in Poppler. Merging four small documents takes about 1 ms, and 1,000 one-page Chrome payslips about 1 s.

PdfPages works on the pages of any existing PDF. Pages are numbered from 1, and ranges are written like "1-3,5,8-" (pages 1 to 3, 5, and 8 to the end): "3,1,2" reorders, "1,1" repeats, "5-3" runs backwards and "last" is the last page. PdfPageRange.Parse reads a range once for reuse; a page past the end throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException ("Page 9 is out of range: the PDF has 5 pages."). byte[] summary = PdfPages.Extract(report, "1-3,5"); // or new[] { 3, 1, 2 } byte[] withoutCover = PdfPages.Remove(report, "1"); byte[] turned = PdfPages.Rotate(scan, 90, "2,4"); // clockwise; null pages = every page byte[][] parts = PdfPages.Split(report, 10); // 10 pages each byte[][] chapters = PdfPages.Split(report, "1-4", "5-9", "10-"); int pages = PdfPages.Count(report); // Encrypted input, files, streams. byte[] page = PdfPages.Extract(secret, "2", new PdfPagesOptions { Password = "pw", Title = "Page 2" }); PdfPages.ExtractFile("report.pdf", "summary.pdf", "1-3"); PdfPages.SplitFile("report.pdf", 1, n => $"report-{n}.pdf"); // Selected pages of several PDFs merged into one (also StreamingPdfMerger.Add(pdf, pages)). byte[] merged = PdfMerger.Merge(new[] { new PdfMergeInput(invoice, "1"), new PdfMergeInput(terms, "2-") }); For the pages taken, the result keeps their content, links and other annotations, the form fields with a widget on them, the bookmarks that go to them, page labels, the document properties and language. Links and bookmarks to pages left out are dropped (a bookmark with a kept bookmark below it stays, without a destination); links between pages taken go to their new place. A tagged input stays tagged: structure elements are kept when some of their content is on a page taken, so a PDF/UA-1 input gives a PDF/UA-1 result (veraPDF passes extracted, removed and split parts). A page taken more than once is copied with its links, but its form fields stay on the first copy and the later copies are not tagged, so such a result no longer claims PDF/UA. Split parses the PDF once for all parts. As with merging, the result is not encrypted and has no signatures.

PdfStamper puts a page of one PDF on top of the pages of another, such as a "PAID" or "COPY" stamp, or underneath them, such as company letterhead. Any PDF can be stamped, not only those PdfPecker made: // A one-page stamp PDF, fitted and centred on every page, half transparent. byte[] paid = PdfStamper.Stamp(invoicePdf, paidStampPdf, new PdfStampOptions { Opacity = 0.5f }); // Letterhead under the content: the stamp's first page on page 1, its second page on all the others. byte[] letter = PdfStamper.Stamp(letterPdf, letterheadPdf, new PdfStampOptions { Underlay = true, MatchPages = true }); // Actual size in the top right corner, 20 pt in from each edge, on the first page only. byte[] copy = PdfStamper.Stamp(pdf, copyStampPdf, new PdfStampOptions { Position = PdfStampPosition.TopRight, Scale = 1, OffsetX = -20, OffsetY = 20, Pages = i => i == 0, }); // The stamp as HTML, rendered at each page's size with no margins. byte[] stamped = PdfStamper.StampHtml(pdf, "
PAID
"); PdfStamper.StampFile("in.pdf", "stamp.pdf", "out.pdf"); PdfStamper.Stamp(inputStream, stampStream, outputStream);

StampPage picks the stamp PDF's page (0-based), Pages the pages to stamp (by 0-based index), Scale the size (0, the default, fits the stamp page on the page keeping its aspect ratio; 1 is its own size), and Position, OffsetX (right) and OffsetY (down) where it goes. The stamp is placed as the page is displayed, so it is upright on rotated pages and sits in the crop box. The stamp page is copied in once as a form XObject, so its text stays text and its graphics stay sharp, however many pages show it. The page's own content is wrapped so a graphics state it leaves behind cannot shift or recolour an overlay. Underlays are hidden by pages that paint an opaque background, and annotations (links, form fields) are always drawn above the page content, overlays included.

Everything else in the document is kept: annotations, form fields and their values, bookmarks, named destinations, attachments, metadata, page labels and the structure tree of a tagged PDF, in which the stamp is marked as an artifact (a PDF/UA-1 document stamped this way still passes veraPDF, as does a PDF/A-2b one when the stamp has embedded fonts). The stamp page's own annotations, form fields and tags are not copied. The result is written out in full, not as an incremental update. A signed PDF is refused with InvalidOperationException, since stamping would break the signatures; set InvalidateSignatures = true to stamp it anyway, or stamp before signing. Encrypted inputs open with Password (and StampPassword for the stamp); the result is not encrypted unless Security is set. Both inputs are handled as untrusted, like merge inputs: damaged files are repaired where possible, decoding is limited, and an unreadable file or one without pages throws InvalidDataException.

PdfToImage and PdfRenderer render PDF pages to PNG, JPEG or WebP (or raw RGBA pixels). This works for any PDF, not only PdfPecker's own output, and also uses no third-party packages: the PDF parser, font engines, JPEG and fax decoders, rasterizer and the PNG, JPEG and WebP encoders are all part of the library. // Every page as PNG bytes (rendered in parallel), or one page (0-based index) byte[][] pages = PdfToImage.Convert(pdfBytes, new ImageOptions { Dpi = 150 }); byte[] first = PdfToImage.ConvertPage(pdfBytes, 0); // report.pdf -> out/report-1.png, out/report-2.png, ... PdfToImage.ConvertFile("report.pdf", "out"); // JPEG or lossless WebP: report.pdf -> out/report-1.jpg, ... (or .webp) PdfToImage.ConvertFile("report.pdf", "out", new ImageOptions { Format = PdfImageFormat.Jpeg, Quality = 90 }); byte[][] webps = PdfToImage.Convert(pdfBytes, new ImageOptions { Format = PdfImageFormat.WebP }); // Open once, render many pages; RenderedImage also exposes the RGBA pixels var renderer = PdfRenderer.Open(pdfBytes, password: null); RenderedImage image = renderer.RenderPage(2, new ImageOptions { Width = 800 }); image.SavePng("page3.png"); File.WriteAllBytes("page3.jpg", image.ToJpeg(quality: 85)); File.WriteAllBytes("page3.webp", image.ToWebP());

Output formats (ImageOptions.Format, default Png; RenderedImage.Encode()/Save() use it too): PNG: lossless, RGB for opaque pages and RGBA otherwise. JPEG: baseline JFIF with the standard (IJG) quantisation tables scaled by Quality (1 to 100, default 85) and Huffman tables optimised per image. Below quality 90 colour is subsampled 4:2:0; from 90 it keeps full resolution (4:4:4), which keeps coloured text sharp. JPEG has no transparency, so a Transparent render is flattened onto BackgroundColor (white by default). At quality 90 a 150 DPI text page decodes at about 45 dB PSNR. WebP: always lossless (VP8L), alpha included, decoding to exactly the PNG's pixels and usually 50% to 70% smaller. Pages with up to 256 colours use a palette (packed 2, 4 or 8 pixels per byte when small); others use subtract-green and per-tile prediction, then LZ77, a colour cache and canonical prefix codes. Here Quality is the compression effort: higher spends more time searching for a smaller file and never changes a pixel. Lossy WebP is not written. WebP is limited to 16,384 pixels per side (JPEG to 65,535); larger images throw NotSupportedException.

ImageOptions sets Dpi (default 150) or a target Width/Height in pixels, BackgroundColor or Transparent, RenderAnnotations, Password, MaxDegreeOfParallelism, PngCompression, Format and Quality (an ArgumentOutOfRangeException outside 1 to 100). A PdfRenderer is thread-safe and shares decoded fonts and images between pages. Encrypted files open with the user or owner password (PdfPasswordException otherwise); unreadable files throw InvalidDataException, as does a page that needs more than 20 million drawing operations (nested forms can multiply a few bytes into billions). Pass a cancellation token to bound the time a page may take.

Files: cross-reference tables and streams, object streams, incremental updates, damaged files (rebuilt by scanning), RC4 and AES-128/256 encryption, all standard filters (Flate, LZW, ASCII85, ASCIIHex, RunLength, predictors). Graphics: paths, fills (non-zero and even-odd), strokes with joins, caps and dashes, clipping, anti-aliasing, all blend modes, constant alpha, soft masks, transparency groups, axial, radial, function and mesh shadings (types 1 to 7), tiling patterns, form XObjects, optional content (layers) and annotation appearances. Text: embedded TrueType, OpenType, CFF and Type 1 fonts, Type 3 fonts, CID fonts with CMaps, vertical text, all text rendering modes. The 14 standard fonts and non-embedded fonts are drawn with built-in Liberation and DejaVu-derived faces stretched to the document's widths. Images: every bit depth and colour space (Gray, RGB, CMYK, Lab, ICC-based, Indexed, Separation, DeviceN), baseline and progressive JPEG, JPEG 2000 (JPXDecode, including embedded alpha), JBIG2 (generic, text, symbol, refinement and halftone regions, with JBIG2Globals), CCITT fax, stencil masks, colour-key masks and soft masks. For what the renderer does not support yet, see Limitations.

PdfPecker is built for fast conversion of HTML templates you control, not for rendering arbitrary web pages. These are the known gaps; most are scope choices for speed and size, and they are the first candidates for future work. Anything not listed in What is supported should be assumed missing.

No JavaScript. Scripts are never run, so content must be in the HTML before conversion (render it server-side first). No network access: http:/https: stylesheets and images are not downloaded. Supply them through your ResourceResolver, as files under BaseDirectory, or as data: URIs. <canvas>, <iframe>, <video>, <audio>, <object> and <embed> are not drawn, nor are file, range, colour and image inputs. Form fields have no JavaScript (no calculations, formats or submit actions), and a field inside a transformed box, a running header or footer, or a position: fixed box is drawn but not fillable.

Without registered fonts or EmbedStandardFonts, text uses the standard PDF fonts, so characters are limited to the Windows-1252 set (Western European languages); other characters are replaced with ?. The bundled Liberation fonts add Central European, Greek and Cyrillic, but not CJK or other scripts: register fonts for those. Complex-script shaping covers Arabic and Hebrew (and other scripts written with Arabic letters, such as Persian and Urdu). Devanagari and other Indic scripts, Thai, Khmer, Myanmar and Syriac are not shaped, so their vowel signs and conjuncts come out wrong, and Thai text breaks only at spaces. There is no vertical text (writing-mode). In Latin and other simple scripts, shaping is limited to pair kerning and standard ligatures; no contextual alternates or other OpenType features (small-caps is synthesized from scaled capitals). Automatic hyphenation (hyphens: auto) has built-in patterns for English, Danish, German, Dutch and Norwegian only; other languages need their patterns in PdfOptions.Hyphenation. hyphenate-limit-chars is not supported. SVG <text> uses only the first value of position lists and has no textPath; in a text chunk with right-to-left text, dx on its tspans is ignored.

A table column width that mixes a percentage with other units (calc(50% - 10px)) is sized as auto. @import is ignored (use ), and rules inside @container blocks are skipped. @page rules for :first, :left and :right pages can style margin boxes but not change the page size or margins. A named page's :first is the document's first page, as in Chrome, not the first page of the named run. Selectors: no ::first-letter/::first-line. A rule with an unsupported selector is skipped. :hover, :focus and similar interaction states never match. Selectors inside :is(), :where() and :not() may have at most eight compound parts (one when nested in another of them). Properties not supported: filter, mix-blend-mode, clip-path on HTML elements (only in SVG), border-image, list-style-image, font-variant-numeric and inset box-shadow. No relative colours (rgb(from …)). text-shadow blur is approximated with faint copies of the text rather than a true Gaussian blur, and decorations (underlines) get no shadow. text-overflow only supports ellipsis at the end of the line (clip and custom strings do nothing). aspect-ratio does not take part in min-/max-content sizing (shrink-to-fit widths) and is ignored on tables. object-fit applies to raster images; an SVG file in keeps its own preserveAspectRatio fit. Borders: groove, ridge, inset and outset draw as solid. position: sticky is drawn as relative; background-attachment: fixed scrolls with the box. Lists: list-style-type covers disc, circle, square, decimal, decimal-leading-zero, alpha, roman and strings only (no Greek, CJK or @counter-style).

No background-clip: text; backgrounds of inline elements (<span>) show only their colour, not images or gradients. Blurred box shadows and repeating gradients with translucent stops are blended onto the background colour rather than truly see-through; SVG gradient stops with transparency are blended onto white.

Grid: no subgrid. Multi-column: children are kept whole and balanced between columns; a single block is never split across columns. Overflow: a positioned child with a z-index inside a clipping box stays stacked within that box.

Images: no AVIF, BMP or TIFF. Animated GIF and WebP files show only their first frame. SVG (inline and files): no embedded <image>. Filters have no feTurbulence, feImage, feTile, feConvolveMatrix, feDisplacementMap or lighting (these pass their input through unchanged) and ignore primitive subregions; filtered content becomes an image (text in it is no longer selectable). Watermark images must be raster images (PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP).

Markdown: no footnotes, definition lists, math or front matter. PdfRenderer (PDF to image): no predefined CJK CMaps or non-embedded CJK fonts, and ICC profiles are not applied (ICC-based colours use their device equivalents). WebP output is lossless only (no lossy VP8), and JPEG output is baseline only (no progressive or arithmetic coding).
PdfPecker lays out documents in your own process, without a browser, so a typical one-page document takes about a millisecond. For memory and CPU per document, see System requirements.

The same three documents converted to A4 PDF by PdfPecker and six .NET alternatives, on one 4-core cloud VM (Intel Xeon @ 2.8 GHz, 16 GB, Linux, .NET 10.0.12). Times are medians after a 3-second warm-up; "first PDF" includes starting the browser where there is one. Parallel runs one conversion per core at once on the 5-page document. Peak memory is the proportional set size (PSS) of the whole process tree, so a browser's helper processes are included once and shared pages are not double-counted. In that run the other converters were up to 70% slower than in the table above and PdfPecker slightly faster, so these two rows are approximate and, if anything, a little slower than a like-for-like run would show. How to read it: PdfPecker is 60 to 150 times faster than the Chromium-based converters on the 1 and 5-page documents and about 14 times faster on the 30-page report, and uses a tenth of their memory. Per-document overhead (a browser tab, a process start) dominates for the others on small documents. Output is not identical. Chromium is the reference for modern CSS and runs JavaScript, which PdfPecker does not. HtmlRenderer supports only HTML 4 and CSS 2 (it drops the invoice's table header colours), and wkhtmltopdf uses a 2016 WebKit, shrinks content to fit by default (24 pages for the report instead of 29) and was archived in 2023. iText pdfHTML lays out the documents itself, like PdfPecker, but its time grows faster than the page count: 242 ms for 5 pages and 4.2 s for the 30-page report, which is one long table. Syncfusion ran as a trial without a licence key, which adds a line of text to each page. Its AdditionalDelay (2 seconds of waiting for scripts by default) was set to 0, as the other Chromium converters don't wait either. With its default settings it scales content down, so the report took 13 pages instead of 29. PDF sizes for the 1 / 5 / 30-page documents: PdfPecker 12 / 26 / 126 KB, Chromium 72 / 139 / 171 KB, wkhtmltopdf 30 / 59 / 191 KB, HtmlRenderer 35 / 65 / 273 KB, iText 26 / 45 / 104 KB, Syncfusion 42 / 89 / 132 KB. Each converter was used the way its documentation suggests for many documents: PdfPecker and HtmlRenderer in process, wkhtmltopdf as one process per document, and PuppeteerSharp and Playwright with one shared browser and a new tab per document (Playwright in one shared browser context, tagged PDF output off for both). iText reuses one font provider per thread, as its knowledge base advises. Syncfusion keeps one converter per concurrent conversion with ReuseBrowserProcess on, as its support forum advises, so the parallel run starts four browsers. IronPDF was not measured here. One user compared PdfPecker with IronPDF 2026.7.2 (Chrome-based) on the 26 templates of their production app, on a 22-core development machine after warm-up: IronPDF took 13.6 s for all 26 documents one at a time and PdfPecker 17 ms (about 800 times faster), and with 22 in parallel IronPDF made 9.2 documents/s and PdfPecker 1,143 (about 125 times). 24 of the 26 documents came out identical; the other two differ by less than 0.25 mm. To reproduce the table from a clone of the PdfPecker repository (needs wkhtmltopdf on PATH and a Chromium at CHROMIUM_PATH): dotnet run --project bench/PdfPecker.Comparison -c Release The comparison project is not part of PdfPecker.sln, so its third-party packages never reach the library or its tests. Your numbers will differ with hardware and documents.

The source paths below are in the PdfPecker repository under src/PdfPecker/. Markdown is first turned into HTML: Markdown/BlockParser finds the block structure line by line, following the CommonMark reference algorithm, Markdown/InlineParser handles emphasis (delimiter stack) and links (bracket stack), and Markdown/HtmlRenderer writes the HTML, which then takes the same path as any other document: Html/HtmlParser builds a DOM in a single pass, applying the browser rules for implied end tags. Css/StyleResolver cascades a user-agent stylesheet, presentational attributes, document stylesheets and inline styles. Rules are indexed by id, class and tag, and elements with identical inputs share one computed style. For a tagged PDF, Pdf/StructureTree then maps the elements to structure types and gives every text node, image and list marker a slot in that tree. Layout/LayoutEngine lays out blocks, inline text (line breaking, justification), lists and tables (automatic column widths), paginating as it goes, and produces a flat list of draw operations. Inline content with right-to-left text gets its embedding levels from Text/Bidi (UAX #9), and each line is put in visual order after it is broken. Fonts/ComplexShaper shapes Arabic and Hebrew runs with the font's GSUB and GPOS tables (Fonts/OpenTypeLayout). Pdf/PdfDocumentWriter writes PDF 1.4: content streams, fonts, image XObjects, link annotations, the bookmark outline and the cross-reference table. A tagged PDF's content is wrapped in marked-content sequences for its slots (or as artifacts), and the structure tree and its parent tree are written last. Fonts/FontSubsetter and Fonts/CffSubsetter cut embedded fonts down to the glyphs used (with their composite components and the CFF subroutines they call). The renderer (Rendering/) works the other way round: Parsing/PdfFile reads the object graph, PageRenderer interprets content streams, Fonts/ turns glyphs into outlines (cached as anti-aliased bitmaps), Images/ decodes images, and Graphics/Rasterizer fills paths with exact area coverage before PngEncoder, JpegEncoder or WebPEncoder writes the result. The third-party fonts, font data and code built into the library are listed, with their licenses, in THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md.
